title: Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning for Offline Settings

en.text: In medicine and education, you rarely get to run experiments. You cannot randomize a treatment on a whim, or re-teach a semester ten different ways to see what sticks. So when reinforcement learning enters these domains, it has to work offline: learn a good decision policy from a fixed batch of experience that someone else already collected. The catch is that the batch only ever records the actions people actually chose, which leaves large parts of the state and action space completely unobserved.

Reinforcement learning needs a model of how the world responds to actions, the transition dynamics T. The textbook move is to estimate T by maximum likelihood (MLE), counting how often each state follows each action. But in the offline setting this estimate is fragile: wherever the data is thin the counts are noisy or missing, and the resulting policy swings wildly from one dataset to the next and confidently recommends actions no one should take. Worse, collecting more data does not fix it. Because the batch reflects an expert who kept choosing good actions, the unhelpful parts of the space stay unexplored no matter how many trajectories you add.

This ICML 2023 paper from Harvard University and Imperial College London turns that limitation into leverage. The people who generated the data, clinicians for instance, were usually acting near-optimally, and their choices quietly encode which actions are good and which are not, information a plain maximum-likelihood fit throws away. The authors introduce Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning (ITL): a gradient-free, constraint-based method that reads a near-optimal expert's decisions as constraints on the dynamics, then clips a Bayesian posterior over T so that every dynamics it keeps yields a safe, high-performing policy.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05075
Why offline dynamics estimation is dangerous

Consider what the maximum-likelihood estimate T_MLE actually sees. For a state-action pair the expert visited many times, the transition counts are reliable. For a pair the expert deliberately avoided, there may be a single sample, or none, and the estimate is essentially a guess. Planning against that guess produces a policy that can pick genuinely bad actions in exactly the regions where the model is least trustworthy.

The paper's ablation drives home an uncomfortable point: this is not a small-sample problem that vanishes with scale. Even in the high-data regime, MLE keeps making what the authors call bad mistakes, actions that fall outside the set the expert would ever consider, because expert-generated data structurally never covers those regions. This is aleatoric uncertainty, not epistemic uncertainty: no amount of the same kind of data removes it.
Reading the expert's choices as constraints

The starting observation is simple. If an expert is near-optimal (formally, epsilon-optimal), then on the states where it commits to a single action, that action must be at least as good as every alternative, up to a small slack epsilon. The paper writes this down exactly. Using the closed-form Bellman equations, which express a policy's value as V = (I - gamma T)^(-1) R, it derives linear constraints on the dynamics requiring that the value of an action the expert took exceeds the value of actions the expert never took.

Any transition model satisfying these constraints reproduces what the authors call the expert's epsilon-ball structure: around each state, the set of actions whose value is within epsilon of the best one. States whose ball contains a single action are deterministic-policy states, while states where several actions tie are stochastic-policy states, a distinction that turns out to matter for how the method is scored.
Clipping the Bayesian posterior

Rather than optimize a single T, ITL stays Bayesian. It places a Dirichlet-Multinomial posterior P(T|D) over the dynamics, the natural conjugate choice for transition counts, and then clips it: draw samples of T, keep only those that satisfy the expert constraints, and discard the rest. The survivors form a new distribution, P(T|D, pi_epsilon), that respects both the data and the expert's demonstrated preferences.

Algorithm 1 makes this concrete with a per-state-action slack term delta that enforces the epsilon-ball property even where the non-linearity of the value function would otherwise break it, and the paper gives separate constraint sets for a fully optimal expert and for a partially uncertain, stochastic-policy one. The whole procedure is gradient-free, which sidesteps the instabilities that earlier gradient-based inverse RL methods inherit in tabular MDPs.
Does it work?

The experiments use a synthetic tabular MDP, small enough to compute everything exactly and probe the method's behavior: 15 states plus a terminal state, 6 actions, and a discount factor of 0.95, with true dynamics deliberately mixed between uniform and highly skewed to create varied behavior. Two coverage regimes, a low-data setting of 15 trajectories and a high-data setting of 300, are crossed with three expert-optimality levels, epsilon = 0, 3, and 4, which respectively leave 0, 3, and 6 stochastic-policy states. Every number below is averaged over 1000 independently generated datasets.

To score a learned policy, the authors use the Q*metric, which sums, over all states, how far the policy's chosen action falls below the true optimal action's value. Lower is better, and zero means the policy is effectively optimal. The figure below shows this metric, dataset by dataset, for the two baselines and for ITL.

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: The picture is stark. Across all six panels the red line, ITL's clipped posterior, sits essentially at zero with a barely visible band of variation. The blue MLE line, by contrast, thrashes between datasets, and the orange unclipped posterior P(T|D) stays high throughout. Keeping the full Bayesian distribution without the expert constraints is actually worse than plain MLE here, because it averages over many dynamics that plan poorly. Only once the expert constraints clip that distribution does it become useful.

en.caption: Table 1. Q*metric (lower is better) across all six regimes. ITL, written P(T|D, pi_epsilon), matches the near-optimal expert and collapses the cross-dataset variance that plagues MLE.

en.text: Table 1 puts numbers on the figure. With a fully optimal expert (epsilon = 0), ITL reaches a Q*metric of exactly 0 ± 0 in both data regimes, against 59.75 for MLE in low data and 142.17 for the unclipped posterior. At the hardest setting (epsilon = 4, high data) it scores 8.79 ± 0.6, beating MLE's 20.11 ± 9.85 and roughly matching the near-optimal expert's own 9.4. The standard deviations are the real story: MLE's spread across datasets is enormous (± 51.99 at epsilon = 0, low data), while ITL's collapses to a fraction of a point. In several settings ITL even edges below the expert that generated the data, recovering a policy slightly better than the demonstrations it learned from.
Accuracy where it counts, and safety everywhere

Beyond the aggregate metric, the paper breaks accuracy down by the kind of state. On deterministic-policy states, where there is a single best action to get right, ITL is correct 100% of the time in every setting, while MLE ranges from 67% to 92% and the unclipped posterior does worse still. Just as important is the a-in-epsilon-balls column: the share of the mistakes a method does make that at least stay inside the expert's epsilon-ball, meaning the chosen action is still near-optimal rather than genuinely harmful. ITL never leaves the epsilon-ball, so by construction it makes no bad mistakes.

en.caption: Table 2. Accuracy and safety in the high-data regime. Deterministic: accuracy on states where the expert has one clearly best action. Stochastic: accuracy on states where several actions are near-optimal. a-in-epsilon-balls: share of mistakes that at least stay within the expert's epsilon-ball (a safe mistake). ITL reaches 100% on deterministic states and never leaves the epsilon-ball.

en.text: The subtler result is on stochastic-policy states. Even though the constraints say nothing explicit about which of several near-optimal actions to pick, ITL is still more accurate there than the baselines, which suggests the constraints implicitly transfer the expert's uncertainty structure into the model rather than only pinning down the single-best-action states.
Why this matters

The practical message is that in offline settings the expert's behavior is not just training data for a policy, it is information about the world model itself. Using it as a constraint on the dynamics buys safety guarantees that neither maximum likelihood nor a plain Bayesian posterior can offer. The resulting policies are gradient-free to compute, provably stay within the expert's safe set, carry dramatically lower variance across datasets, and can even outperform the expert who produced the data. The same constraints-plus-uncertainty recipe also yields a ranking of actions in the uncertain states, exactly the kind of informative, hedged recommendation that high-stakes planning in healthcare would want.

The honest boundaries: the study is on a small synthetic tabular MDP, and the method assumes the reward function R is known and that the demonstrating expert really is near-optimal. Whether the same clipping idea scales to large or continuous state spaces, and how sensitive it is to a genuinely sub-optimal expert, is left for future work. But as a statement of principle, ITL makes a clean case that the choices already sitting in your offline data are a constraint worth enforcing rather than a signal to average away.

zh.text: 在医疗和教育这样的领域，我们几乎没有随意做实验的机会：不能凭一时兴起就随机分配某种治疗方案，也不能把一个学期重上十遍，看哪种教法更有效。因此当强化学习进入这些场景时，它必须以离线（offline）的方式工作，也就是从别人已经收集好的一批固定经验中学出一个好策略。麻烦在于，这批数据只记录了人们真正采取过的动作，状态与动作空间中很大一部分从未被观察到。

强化学习需要一个描述世界如何对动作作出反应的模型，也就是转移动态（transition dynamics）T。教科书式的做法是用极大似然（MLE）来估计 T，统计每个状态在每个动作之后转移到各处的频次。但在离线设定下，这个估计非常脆弱：凡是数据稀疏的地方，计数要么噪声很大、要么根本缺失，得到的策略会在不同数据集之间剧烈摇摆，并自信地推荐一些本不该采取的动作。更糟的是，多收集数据也解决不了问题：因为这批数据来自一个始终在选择好动作的专家，那些无用的区域无论再增加多少条轨迹都不会被探索到。

这篇来自哈佛大学与帝国理工学院的 ICML 2023 论文，把这一局限转化成了优势。生成数据的人（比如临床医生）通常都在接近最优地行动，他们的选择悄悄编码了哪些动作好、哪些不好，而这恰恰是朴素极大似然完全丢弃掉的信息。作者提出了贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL）：一种无需梯度、基于约束的方法，它把近最优专家的决策读作对动态的约束，再对 T 的贝叶斯后验进行“裁剪”，使得保留下来的每一个动态都能给出安全且高性能的策略。
论文地址：https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05075
为什么离线估计动态很危险
想想极大似然估计 T_MLE 究竟看到了什么。对于专家反复访问过的状态-动作对，转移计数是可靠的；而对于专家刻意回避的状态-动作对，可能只有一个样本、甚至一个都没有，此时的估计基本靠猜。用这样的估计去做规划，就会在模型最不可信的区域里恰恰选出真正糟糕的动作。
论文的消融实验点出了一个令人不安的事实：这并不是一个随着规模增大就会消失的小样本问题。即便在高数据规模下，MLE 依然会犯作者所说的“坏错误”（bad mistakes），也就是选择那些落在专家绝不会考虑的集合之外的动作，因为专家生成的数据在结构上就永远覆盖不到这些区域。这是偶然不确定性（aleatoric uncertainty），而非认知不确定性：同一种数据再多，也无法消除它。
把专家的选择读作约束

出发点很简单。如果一个专家是近最优的（形式化地说，是 epsilon 最优的），那么在它只选择单一动作的状态上，这个动作至少要和其他所有备选一样好，最多相差一个很小的松弛量 epsilon。论文把这一点精确地写了下来。借助闭式的 Bellman 方程，也就是把策略价值表示为 V^π = (I − γT_π)^{-1} R_π，作者推导出对动态的线性约束：要求专家采取过的动作，其价值高于专家从未采取过的动作。

任何满足这些约束的转移模型，都会重现作者所称的专家 epsilon 球（epsilon-ball）结构：在每个状态周围，价值与最优动作相差不超过 epsilon 的那组动作。epsilon 球中只含单一动作的状态称为确定性策略状态（deterministic-policy states），多个动作并列的状态则称为随机性策略状态（stochastic-policy states）。这个区分，对于该方法如何被评估至关重要。
裁剪贝叶斯后验
ITL 并不去优化单一的 T，而是保持贝叶斯视角。它在动态上放置一个 Dirichlet-Multinomial 后验 P(T|D)，这是转移计数的自然共轭选择，然后对它进行裁剪：从中采样若干个 T，只保留满足专家约束的那些，其余全部丢弃。留存下来的样本构成一个新的分布 P(T|D, πε)，它同时尊重数据和专家展示出来的偏好。
算法 1 将这一过程具体化，并为每个状态-动作引入一个松弛项 delta，即使在价值函数非线性、否则会破坏 epsilon 球性质的地方也能强制保持该性质；论文还分别给出了面向完全最优专家、以及面向部分不确定（随机性策略）专家的两套约束。整个流程无需梯度，从而绕开了以往基于梯度的逆强化学习方法在表格型 MDP 上固有的不稳定性。
它有效吗？

实验采用一个合成的表格型 MDP，规模小到足以精确计算一切、细致考察方法的行为：15 个状态外加一个终止状态、6 个动作、折扣因子 0.95，真实动态被刻意设计为在均匀与高度偏斜之间混合，以制造多样的行为。两种覆盖规模，低数据为 15 条轨迹、高数据为 300 条，与三种专家最优程度 epsilon = 0、3、4 交叉，后者分别留下 0、3、6 个随机性策略状态。下面的每个数字，都是在 1000 个独立生成的数据集上平均得到的。
为了给学到的策略打分，作者使用 Q*metric：它在所有状态上累加策略所选动作的价值比真实最优动作低多少。数值越低越好，为零意味着策略实际上已达到最优。下图逐个数据集地展示了这一指标，分别绘制两条基线以及本文方法 ITL 的曲线以作对比。

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 结果非常鲜明。在全部六个子图中，红线（ITL 裁剪后的后验）基本贴着零，波动带几乎看不见；相比之下，蓝色的 MLE 线在数据集之间剧烈跳动，橙色的未裁剪后验 P(T|D) 则始终居高不下。在这里，保留完整的贝叶斯分布却不加专家约束，反而比朴素 MLE 更差，因为它把许多规划表现很差的动态一并平均了进来。只有当专家约束把这个分布裁剪之后，它才真正变得有用。

zh.caption: 表1 六种设置下的 Q*metric（越低越好）。ITL（写作 P(T|D, πε)）达到接近最优专家的水平，并消除了困扰 MLE 的跨数据集方差。

zh.text: 表1 给这张图配上了具体数字。面对完全最优的专家（epsilon = 0），ITL 在两种数据规模下都达到恰好 0 ± 0 的 Q*metric，而低数据下 MLE 为 59.75、未裁剪后验高达 142.17。在最难的设置（epsilon = 4，高数据）下，ITL 得到 8.79 ± 0.6，优于 MLE 的 20.11 ± 9.85，并大致追平近最优专家自身的 9.4。真正的看点在标准差：MLE 在不同数据集之间的波动极大（epsilon = 0、低数据时达到 ± 51.99），而 ITL 的波动收缩到不足一分。在若干设置下，ITL 甚至略微超过了生成数据的专家，学出了比示范本身更好一点的策略。
在关键处准确，在各处安全

除了聚合指标，论文还按状态类型拆解了准确率。在确定性策略状态（只有唯一最优动作需要答对）上，ITL 在每一种设置下都是 100% 正确，而 MLE 在 67% 到 92% 之间波动，未裁剪后验则更差。同样重要的是 a ∈ epsilon 球这一列：它衡量一个方法所犯的错误中，有多少至少仍落在专家的 epsilon 球之内，也就是所选动作依然接近最优、而非真正有害。ITL 从不离开 epsilon 球，因此在构造上就不会犯坏错误。

zh.caption: 表2 高数据规模下的准确率与安全性。确定性（Deterministic）：专家有唯一最优动作的状态上的准确率；随机性（Stochastic）：多个动作都接近最优的状态上的准确率；a ∈ epsilon 球：所犯错误中仍落在专家 epsilon 球内的“安全错误”所占比例。ITL 在确定性状态上达到 100%，且从不离开 epsilon 球。

zh.text: 更微妙的结果出现在随机性策略状态上。尽管约束并没有明确指定在多个近最优动作中该选哪一个，ITL 在这些状态上仍然比基线更准确，这表明约束把专家的不确定性结构隐式地传递进了模型，而不只是钉住那些只有单一最优动作的状态。
这为什么重要

务实的结论是：在离线设定中，专家的行为不仅仅是训练策略的数据，它本身就是关于世界模型的信息。把它当作对动态的约束，能换来极大似然和朴素贝叶斯后验都给不了的安全保证。由此得到的策略在计算上无需梯度，可证明地停留在专家的安全集合之内，在不同数据集之间方差大幅降低，甚至能超过生成数据的专家。同一套“约束加不确定性”的配方，还能在不确定的状态上给出动作排序，这正是医疗等高风险规划所需要的、有信息量又留有余地的推荐。
诚实地说明边界：本研究基于一个小规模的合成表格型 MDP，且方法假设奖励函数 R 已知、示范专家确实近最优；裁剪思想能否扩展到大规模或连续状态空间、以及它对真正次优专家的敏感度，都留待未来工作。但原则很清楚：离线数据里已经存在的那些选择，是一条值得强制执行的约束，而不是应当被平均掉的信号。

zh.subtitle: 哈佛大学与帝国理工学院提出贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL），一种无需梯度、把近最优专家的决策转化为对世界模型硬约束的方法。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: Why offline dynamics estimation is dangerous

Consider what the maximum-likelihood estimate T_MLE actually sees. For a state-action pair the expert visited many times, the transition counts are reliable. For a pair the expert deliberately avoided, there may be a single sample, or none, and the estimate is essentially a guess. Planning against that guess produces a policy that can pick genuinely bad actions in exactly the regions where the model is least trustworthy.

The paper's ablation drives home an uncomfortable point: this is not a small-sample problem that vanishes with scale. Even in the high-data regime, MLE keeps making what the authors call bad mistakes, actions that fall outside the set the expert would ever consider, because expert-generated data structurally never covers those regions. This is aleatoric uncertainty, not epistemic uncertainty: no amount of the same kind of data removes it.

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 为什么离线估计动态很危险
想想极大似然估计 T_MLE 究竟看到了什么。对于专家反复访问过的状态-动作对，转移计数是可靠的；而对于专家刻意回避的状态-动作对，可能只有一个样本、甚至一个都没有，此时的估计基本靠猜。用这样的估计去做规划，就会在模型最不可信的区域里恰恰选出真正糟糕的动作。
论文的消融实验点出了一个令人不安的事实：这并不是一个随着规模增大就会消失的小样本问题。即便在高数据规模下，MLE 依然会犯作者所说的“坏错误”（bad mistakes），也就是选择那些落在专家绝不会考虑的集合之外的动作，因为专家生成的数据在结构上就永远覆盖不到这些区域。这是偶然不确定性（aleatoric uncertainty），而非认知不确定性：同一种数据再多，也无法消除它。

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 数据再多也救不了 MLE：用专家的选择约束离线强化学习的世界模型
zh.subtitle: 哈佛大学与帝国理工学院提出贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL），一种无需梯度、把近最优专家的决策转化为对世界模型硬约束的方法。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: Reading the expert's choices as constraints

The starting observation is simple. If an expert is near-optimal (formally, epsilon-optimal), then on the states where it commits to a single action, that action must be at least as good as every alternative, up to a small slack epsilon. The paper writes this down exactly. Using the closed-form Bellman equations, which express a policy's value as V = (I - gamma T)^(-1) R, it derives linear constraints on the dynamics requiring that the value of an action the expert took exceeds the value of actions the expert never took.

Any transition model satisfying these constraints reproduces what the authors call the expert's epsilon-ball structure: around each state, the set of actions whose value is within epsilon of the best one. States whose ball contains a single action are deterministic-policy states, while states where several actions tie are stochastic-policy states, a distinction that turns out to matter for how the method is scored.

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 把专家的选择读作约束

出发点很简单。如果一个专家是近最优的（形式化地说，是 epsilon 最优的），那么在它只选择单一动作的状态上，这个动作至少要和其他所有备选一样好，最多相差一个很小的松弛量 epsilon。论文把这一点精确地写了下来。借助闭式的 Bellman 方程，也就是把策略价值表示为 V^π = (I − γT_π)^{-1} R_π，作者推导出对动态的线性约束：要求专家采取过的动作，其价值高于专家从未采取过的动作。

任何满足这些约束的转移模型，都会重现作者所称的专家 epsilon 球（epsilon-ball）结构：在每个状态周围，价值与最优动作相差不超过 epsilon 的那组动作。epsilon 球中只含单一动作的状态称为确定性策略状态（deterministic-policy states），多个动作并列的状态则称为随机性策略状态（stochastic-policy states）。这个区分，对于该方法如何被评估至关重要。

zh.subtitle: 哈佛大学与帝国理工学院提出贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL），一种无需梯度、把近最优专家的决策转化为对世界模型硬约束的方法。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: In medicine and education, you rarely get to run experiments. You cannot randomize a treatment on a whim, or re-teach a semester ten different ways to see what sticks. So when reinforcement learning enters these domains, it has to work offline: learn a good decision policy from a fixed batch of experience that someone else already collected. The catch is that the batch only ever records the actions people actually chose, which leaves large parts of the state and action space completely unobserved.

Reinforcement learning needs a model of how the world responds to actions, the transition dynamics T. The textbook move is to estimate T by maximum likelihood (MLE), counting how often each state follows each action. But in the offline setting this estimate is fragile: wherever the data is thin the counts are noisy or missing, and the resulting policy swings wildly from one dataset to the next and confidently recommends actions no one should take. Worse, collecting more data does not fix it. Because the batch reflects an expert who kept choosing good actions, the unhelpful parts of the space stay unexplored no matter how many trajectories you add.

This ICML 2023 paper from Harvard University and Imperial College London turns that limitation into leverage. The people who generated the data, clinicians for instance, were usually acting near-optimally, and their choices quietly encode which actions are good and which are not, information a plain maximum-likelihood fit throws away. The authors introduce Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning (ITL): a gradient-free, constraint-based method that reads a near-optimal expert's decisions as constraints on the dynamics, then clips a Bayesian posterior over T so that every dynamics it keeps yields a safe, high-performing policy.
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05075
Reading the expert's choices as constraints

The starting observation is simple. If an expert is near-optimal (formally, epsilon-optimal), then on the states where it commits to a single action, that action must be at least as good as every alternative, up to a small slack epsilon. Using the closed-form Bellman equations, which express a policy's value as V = (I - gamma T)^(-1) R, it derives linear constraints on the dynamics requiring that the value of an action the expert took exceeds the value of actions the expert never took.

Any transition model satisfying these constraints reproduces what the authors call the expert's epsilon-ball structure: around each state, the set of actions whose value is within epsilon of the best one. States whose ball contains a single action are deterministic-policy states, while states where several actions tie are stochastic-policy states, a distinction that turns out to matter for how the method is scored.

zh.text: 在医疗和教育这样的领域，我们几乎没有随意做实验的机会：不能凭一时兴起就随机分配某种治疗方案，也不能把一个学期重上十遍，看哪种教法更有效。因此当强化学习进入这些场景时，它必须以离线（offline）的方式工作，也就是从别人已经收集好的一批固定经验中学出一个好策略。麻烦在于，这批数据只记录了人们真正采取过的动作，状态与动作空间中很大一部分从未被观察到。

强化学习需要一个描述世界如何对动作作出反应的模型，也就是转移动态（transition dynamics）T。教科书式的做法是用极大似然（MLE）来估计 T，统计每个状态在每个动作之后转移到各处的频次。但在离线设定下，这个估计非常脆弱：凡是数据稀疏的地方，计数要么噪声很大、要么根本缺失，得到的策略会在不同数据集之间剧烈摇摆，并自信地推荐一些本不该采取的动作。更糟的是，多收集数据也解决不了问题：因为这批数据来自一个始终在选择好动作的专家，那些无用的区域无论再增加多少条轨迹都不会被探索到。

这篇来自哈佛大学与帝国理工学院的 ICML 2023 论文，把这一局限转化成了优势。生成数据的人（比如临床医生）通常都在接近最优地行动，他们的选择悄悄编码了哪些动作好、哪些不好，而这恰恰是朴素极大似然完全丢弃掉的信息。作者提出了贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL）：一种无需梯度、基于约束的方法，它把近最优专家的决策读作对动态的约束，再对 T 的贝叶斯后验进行“裁剪”，使得保留下来的每一个动态都能给出安全且高性能的策略。
论文地址：https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05075

Accuracy where it counts, and safety everywhere

Beyond the aggregate metric, the paper breaks accuracy down by the kind of state. On deterministic-policy states, where there is a single best action to get right, ITL is correct 100% of the time in every setting, while MLE ranges from 67% to 92% and the unclipped posterior does worse still. Just as important is the a-in-epsilon-balls column: the share of the mistakes a method does make that at least stay inside the expert's epsilon-ball, meaning the chosen action is still near-optimal rather than genuinely harmful. ITL never leaves the epsilon-ball, so by construction it makes no bad mistakes.

en.caption: Table 2. Accuracy and safety in the high-data regime. Deterministic: accuracy on states where the expert has one clearly best action. Stochastic: accuracy on states where several actions are near-optimal. a-in-epsilon-balls: share of mistakes that at least stay within the expert's epsilon-ball (a safe mistake). ITL reaches 100% on deterministic states and never leaves the epsilon-ball.

en.text: The subtler result is on stochastic-policy states. Even though the constraints say nothing explicit about which of several near-optimal actions to pick, ITL is still more accurate there than the baselines, which suggests the constraints implicitly transfer the expert's uncertainty structure into the model rather than only pinning down the single-best-action states.

zh.text: 它有效吗？

实验采用一个合成的表格型 MDP，规模小到足以精确计算一切、细致考察方法的行为：15 个状态外加一个终止状态、6 个动作、折扣因子 0.95，真实动态被刻意设计为在均匀与高度偏斜之间混合，以制造多样的行为。两种覆盖规模，低数据为 15 条轨迹、高数据为 300 条，与三种专家最优程度 epsilon = 0、3、4 交叉，后者分别留下 0、3、6 个随机性策略状态。下面的每个数字，都是在 1000 个独立生成的数据集上平均得到的。
为了给学到的策略打分，作者使用 Q*metric：它在所有状态上累加策略所选动作的价值比真实最优动作低多少。数值越低越好，为零意味着策略实际上已达到最优。下图逐个数据集地展示了这一指标，分别绘制两条基线以及本文方法 ITL 的曲线以作对比。

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 结果非常鲜明。在全部六个子图中，红线（ITL 裁剪后的后验）基本贴着零，波动带几乎看不见；相比之下，蓝色的 MLE 线在数据集之间剧烈跳动，橙色的未裁剪后验 P(T|D) 则始终居高不下。在这里，保留完整的贝叶斯分布却不加专家约束，反而比朴素 MLE 更差，因为它把许多规划表现很差的动态一并平均了进来。只有当专家约束把这个分布裁剪之后，它才真正变得有用。

zh.caption: 表1 六种设置下的 Q*metric（越低越好）。ITL（写作 P(T|D, πε)）达到接近最优专家的水平，并消除了困扰 MLE 的跨数据集方差。

zh.text: 表1 给这张图配上了具体数字。面对完全最优的专家（epsilon = 0），ITL 在两种数据规模下都达到恰好 0 ± 0 的 Q*metric，而低数据下 MLE 为 59.75、未裁剪后验高达 142.17。在最难的设置（epsilon = 4，高数据）下，ITL 得到 8.79 ± 0.6，优于 MLE 的 20.11 ± 9.85，并大致追平近最优专家自身的 9.4。真正的看点在标准差：MLE 在不同数据集之间的波动极大（epsilon = 0、低数据时达到 ± 51.99），而 ITL 的波动收缩到不足一分。在若干设置下，ITL 甚至略微超过了生成数据的专家，学出了比示范本身更好一点的策略。
在关键处准确，在各处安全

除了聚合指标，论文还按状态类型拆解了准确率。在确定性策略状态（只有唯一最优动作需要答对）上，ITL 在每一种设置下都是 100% 正确，而 MLE 在 67% 到 92% 之间波动，未裁剪后验则更差。同样重要的是 a ∈ epsilon 球这一列：它衡量一个方法所犯的错误中，有多少至少仍落在专家的 epsilon 球之内，也就是所选动作依然接近最优、而非真正有害。ITL 从不离开 epsilon 球，因此在构造上就不会犯坏错误。

zh.caption: 表2 高数据规模下的准确率与安全性。确定性（Deterministic）：专家有唯一最优动作的状态上的准确率；随机性（Stochastic）：多个动作都接近最优的状态上的准确率；a ∈ epsilon 球：所犯错误中仍落在专家 epsilon 球内的“安全错误”所占比例。ITL 在确定性状态上达到 100%，且从不离开 epsilon 球。

zh.text: 更微妙的结果出现在随机性策略状态上。尽管约束并没有明确指定在多个近最优动作中该选哪一个，ITL 在这些状态上仍然比基线更准确，这表明约束把专家的不确定性结构隐式地传递进了模型，而不只是钉住那些只有单一最优动作的状态。

en.title: ICML 2023 | When More Data Won't Save an Offline Policy: Learning Safe Dynamics From Expert Choices
en.subtitle: Harvard University and Imperial College London introduce Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning (ITL), a gradient-free way to turn a near-optimal expert's decisions into hard constraints on an offline model of the world.

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 数据再多也救不了 MLE：用专家的选择约束离线强化学习的世界模型
zh.subtitle: 哈佛大学与帝国理工学院提出贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL），一种无需梯度、把近最优专家的决策转化为对世界模型硬约束的方法。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: Why offline dynamics estimation is dangerous

Consider what the maximum-likelihood estimate T_MLE actually sees. For a state-action pair the expert visited many times, the transition counts are reliable. For a pair the expert deliberately avoided, there may be a single sample, or none, and the estimate is essentially a guess. Planning against that guess produces a policy that can pick genuinely bad actions in exactly the regions where the model is least trustworthy.

The paper's ablation drives home an uncomfortable point: this is not a small-sample problem that vanishes with scale. Even in the high-data regime, MLE keeps making what the authors call bad mistakes, actions that fall outside the set the expert would ever consider, because expert-generated data structurally never covers those regions. This is aleatoric uncertainty, not epistemic uncertainty: no amount of the same kind of data removes it.

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 在医疗和教育这样的领域，我们几乎没有随意做实验的机会：不能凭一时兴起就随机分配某种治疗方案，也不能把一个学期重上十遍，看哪种教法更有效。因此当强化学习进入这些场景时，它必须以离线（offline）的方式工作，也就是从别人已经收集好的一批固定经验中学出一个好策略。麻烦在于，这批数据只记录了人们真正采取过的动作，状态与动作空间中很大一部分从未被观察到。

强化学习需要一个描述世界如何对动作作出反应的模型，也就是转移动态（transition dynamics）T。教科书式的做法是用极大似然（MLE）来估计 T，统计每个状态在每个动作之后转移到各处的频次。但在离线设定下，这个估计非常脆弱：凡是数据稀疏的地方，计数要么噪声很大、要么根本缺失，得到的策略会在不同数据集之间剧烈摇摆，并自信地推荐一些本不该采取的动作。更糟的是，多收集数据也解决不了问题：因为这批数据来自一个始终在选择好动作的专家，那些无用的区域无论再增加多少条轨迹都不会被探索到。

这篇来自哈佛大学与帝国理工学院的 ICML 2023 论文，把这一局限转化成了优势。生成数据的人（比如临床医生）通常都在接近最优地行动，他们的选择悄悄编码了哪些动作好、哪些不好，而这恰恰是朴素极大似然完全丢弃掉的信息。作者提出了贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL）：一种无需梯度、基于约束的方法，它把近最优专家的决策读作对动态的约束，再对 T 的贝叶斯后验进行“裁剪”，使得保留下来的每一个动态都能给出安全且高性能的策略。
论文地址：https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05075

en.title: ICML 2023 | When More Data Won't Save an Offline Policy: Learning Safe Dynamics From Expert Choices
en.subtitle: Harvard University and Imperial College London introduce Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning (ITL), a gradient-free way to turn a near-optimal expert's decisions into hard constraints on an offline model of the world.

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 数据再多也救不了 MLE：用专家的选择约束离线强化学习的世界模型
zh.subtitle: 哈佛大学与帝国理工学院提出贝叶斯逆转移学习（Bayesian Inverse Transition Learning, ITL），一种无需梯度、把近最优专家的决策转化为对世界模型硬约束的方法。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Q*metric across 1000 datasets for three ways of estimating the transition dynamics, under three expert-optimality levels (epsilon = 0, 3, 4) and two data regimes. Lower is better. The red line (ITL, our clipped posterior) hugs zero with almost no spread, while MLE (blue) swings violently from dataset to dataset and the unclipped Bayesian posterior (orange) sits far higher throughout.

en.text: Why this matters

The practical message is that in offline settings the expert's behavior is not just training data for a policy, it is information about the world model itself. Using it as a constraint on the dynamics buys safety guarantees that neither maximum likelihood nor a plain Bayesian posterior can offer. The resulting policies are gradient-free to compute, provably stay within the expert's safe set, carry dramatically lower variance across datasets, and can even outperform the expert who produced the data. The same constraints-plus-uncertainty recipe also yields a ranking of actions in the uncertain states, exactly the kind of informative, hedged recommendation that high-stakes planning in healthcare would want.

The honest boundaries: the study is on a small synthetic tabular MDP, and the method assumes the reward function R is known and that the demonstrating expert really is near-optimal. Whether the same clipping idea scales to large or continuous state spaces, and how sensitive it is to a genuinely sub-optimal expert, is left for future work. But as a statement of principle, ITL makes a clean case that the choices already sitting in your offline data are a constraint worth enforcing rather than a signal to average away.

zh.caption: 图1 三种估计转移动态的方法在 1000 个数据集上的 Q*metric，覆盖三种专家最优程度（epsilon = 0、3、4）与两种数据规模。数值越低越好。红线（ITL，我们裁剪后的后验）几乎贴着零、波动极小；而 MLE（蓝线）在数据集之间剧烈震荡，未裁剪的贝叶斯后验（橙线）则始终高得多。

zh.text: 这为什么重要

务实的结论是：在离线设定中，专家的行为不仅仅是训练策略的数据，它本身就是关于世界模型的信息。把它当作对动态的约束，能换来极大似然和朴素贝叶斯后验都给不了的安全保证。由此得到的策略在计算上无需梯度，可证明地停留在专家的安全集合之内，在不同数据集之间方差大幅降低，甚至能超过生成数据的专家。同一套“约束加不确定性”的配方，还能在不确定的状态上给出动作排序，这正是医疗等高风险规划所需要的、有信息量又留有余地的推荐。
诚实地说明边界：本研究基于一个小规模的合成表格型 MDP，且方法假设奖励函数 R 已知、示范专家确实近最优；裁剪思想能否扩展到大规模或连续状态空间、以及它对真正次优专家的敏感度，都留待未来工作。但原则很清楚：离线数据里已经存在的那些选择，是一条值得强制执行的约束，而不是应当被平均掉的信号。
